DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
 
 
 
Timely Petition for Review having been filed by the Respondent herein and notice given 
to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issue(s) of accident, causal connection, 
jurisdiction, and proper party (Petitioner), and being advised of the facts and law, affirms and 
adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is attached hereto and made a part hereof. This case 
was consolidated with case number 08WC055283, for which the Commission has issued a 
separate Decision. 
 
 
 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed September 30, 2025 is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
 
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent pay to 
Petitioner interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
 
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent shall have 
credit for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of the Petitioner on account of said accidental 
injury.

An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Crystal L. Caison, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city of 
Chicago, on July 8, 2025. After reviewing all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes 
findings on the disputed issues checked below and attaches those findings to this document.  
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
A. 
 Was Respondent operating under and subject to the Illinois Workers' Compensation or Occupational  
 
 
  Diseases Act? 
 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
 
C. 
 Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Decedent's employment by Respondent? 
 
D. 
 What was the date of the accident? 
 
E. 
 Was timely notice of the accident given to Respondent? 
 
F. 
 Is Decedent's current condition of ill-being causally related to the injury? 
 
G. 
 What were Decedent's earnings? 
 
H. 
 What was Decedent's age at the time of the accident? 
 
I. 
 What was Decedent's marital status at the time of the accident? 
 
J. 
 Who was dependent on Decedent at the time of death? 
 
K. 
 Were the medical services that were provided to Decedent reasonable and necessary? Has Respondent  
 paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
 
L. 
 What compensation for permanent disability, if any, is due? 
 
M. 
 Should penalties or fees be imposed upon Respondent? 
 
N. 
 Is Respondent due any credit? 
 
O. 
 Other  Jurisdiction of the IWCC and Proper Party Petitioner

FINDINGS 
 
On the date of accident, 1/23/2006, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Decedent and Respondent.   
 
In the year preceding the injury, Decedent earned $79,098.00; the average weekly wage was $1,521.12. 
 
On the date of accident, Decedent was 68 years of age, married with 3 dependent children. 
 
 
Respondent shall be given a credit of $0 for TTD, $0 for TPD, $0 for maintenance, and $0 for other benefits, 
for a total credit of $0. 
 
 
 
 
ORDER 
 
Based on the stipulation of the parties, the Arbitrator renders all issues moot under Case # 08WC55917.  See 
Arbitrator’s Decision and Order under Case #08WC55283 for conclusions of law and findings. 
 
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this 
decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the 
decision of the Commission.   
 
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice 
of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; however, 
if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not accrue.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 
 
This matter proceeded to hearing on July 8, 2025, before Arbitrator Crystal L. Caison with 
consolidated case 08WC55917, which is brought by Victoria Coda “on behalf of Decedent”. The 
issues in dispute for case #08WC55917 are accident, causal connection, and “jurisdiction of the 
IWCC and proper party petitioner”. Arbitrator’s Exhibit (“AX1”) The Parties stipulated that no 
claim was being made in case #08WC55917 for temporary total disability benefits, medical 
expenses, permanent partial or total disability, or any other accrued benefits Decedent may have 
been entitled to prior to his death. 
 
Case #08WC55283 is brought pursuant to section 7(a) by Petitioner, Victoria Coda 
(“Coda” and “Petitioner”) as widow and surviving spouse of Stephen Coda (“Decedent”), and as 
mother and next friend of Jennifer Coda (“J.”), Tyler Coda (“T.”), and Kyle Coda (“K.”) as the 
surviving dependents of Decedent. The issues in dispute for Case #08WC55283 are accident, 
causal connection, and “other” issues of death benefits, burial expenses. Arbitrator’s Exhibit 
(“AX2”)  
 
 
 
26IWCC0131

 
Consolidated Case: Robert Stephen Coda (deceased) by Widow Victoria L. Coda 
 
 
 
Case # 08 WC55917 
 
2 
 
 
All benefits being sought are pursuant to Section 7 of the Act as death benefits being 
brought by Decedent’s widow and heirs in their own capacities in case 08WC55283. Based upon 
the Parties’ stipulation that no benefits are sought in 08WC55917, the Arbitrator finds that the 
issues in that case are moot.  
 
 This consolidated decision will address all issues in case #08WC55283. Notwithstanding, 
the issues in case #08WC55917 being rendered moot, a separate order will be issued for each 
case. In this decision, the terms, Petitioner and Decedent are interchangeable. 
 
 
THE ARBITRATOR MAKES THE FOLLOWING FINDINGS OF FACT: 
Testimony of Kathy Suoranta, Former Colleague of Decedent 
Kathy Suoranta testified on behalf of Petitioner. Suoranta worked for IDOR from 1986 
until 2012 as a Senior Special Agent. Suoranta worked with the Decedent at IDOR. Decedent had 
been a Senior Special Agent and he and Suoranta were partners for several years. She could not 
recall how many years they worked together.  
Her job duties involved investigating individuals and businesses regarding their taxes. She 
would interview witnesses, analyze records, and, when necessary, execute search warrants and 
arrest people. IDOR agents normally worked with partners, particularly when someone needed to 
be interviewed, so there would be a witness. Her job duties would vary, but typically agents would 
wear regular business attire and would carry guns. They would wear Kevlar vests if a search 
warrant was being executed, or an arrest was expected. Suoranta indicated that Agents working 
on “revocations” might more frequently wear Kevlar vests due to the confrontational nature of 
those assignments. Revocations occurred when a business license was revoked but the company 
failed to cease operations. The civil side of IDOR would ask for assistance to remind the business 
owner that they could no longer operate. Suoranta indicated that, at times, revocations could be 
more stressful assignments because of the reactions of business owners to the revocation process. 
Suoranta never performed “revocations” during her tenure with IDOR. She testified that Decedent 
had worked on revocations but that she did not know the volume of revocation assignments he 
worked.  
Suoranta testified that in 2005 and 2006, IDOR underwent internal changes, and that there 
were periods when no permanent supervisor was assigned to their department. During that time,

senior special agents would serve as temporary supervisors of the department. Both herself and 
Decedent temporarily filled that role. This would involve more managerial tasks than normal. 
Suoranta did not testify as to the duration or frequency with which either her or the decedent filled 
this role.  
Suoranta was not with the Decedent at the time of the accident on January 23, 2006. She 
saw him in the office that morning and he “seemed fine,” with “nothing unusual to note.” 
Decedent was not wearing a Kevlar vest when Suoranta saw him, but she indicated that most 
agents would leave their vest inside their vehicle until an assignment required them to wear it. 
Suoranta recalled that Decedent left the office, and she assumed he went out on assignment, but 
admitted that she did not know what assignment he may have been given that date, whether it 
involved a revocation or where he was going.  
Testimony of Victoria Coda, Petitioner and Widow of Decedent 
Victoria Coda testified that she and Decedent were married on June 6, 1992. PX15 Coda 
has not remarried since her husband’s passing and is not currently engaged. She described 
Decedent’s personality as straightforward, always very professional, business like, and never 
wanting her to worry about him. Decedent was an agent with IDOR at the time of his passing in 
2006. 
Coda has no first-hand knowledge of Decedent’s responsibilities at IDOR. She testified 
that Decedent’s job seemed to become more demanding between 2005 to 2006, as she recalled 
that he was spending more time after normal work hours logging his assignment notes and was 
working later, causing them to hold dinner for him frequently. Decedent had worked weekends 
in the past, but Coda noticed that Decedent started working more weekends than usual around 
Fall 2005. She testified that he would take his gun with him when he went on Weekend 
assignments. Coda did not know what sort of projects or assignments Decedent worked on. He 
did not tell her, and she did not ask. She testified that she confronted Decedent about his increasing 
work hours in November 2005. She testified that Decedent “sugarcoated everything” because he 
did not want her to worry about him.  
Coda testified that Decedent had previously undergone a heart stint surgery approximately 
a decade prior to 2006. RX4 Decedent had needed regular follow-up visits since then. She 
believed Decedent had been in good health on the morning of January 23, 2006, a Monday. Coda

recalled that it seemed like a “normal morning” and Decedent had kissed her and their daughter 
goodbye, tipped his hat, and left. Later that day three IDOR agents came to her home to inform 
her of Decedent’s heart attack and take her to the hospital to see him. After several days in-patient 
at Palos Community Hospital, Petitioner passed away on February 1, 2006. PX9 Coda 
subsequently handled arrangements for his funeral and burial, incurring expenses totaling 
$9,698.23. PX8  
Coda and Decedent had three children together before his passing. PX10 Decedent had no 
other children. At the time of his death on February 1, 2006, all three of their children were under 
the age of majority. Id. K., their oldest, graduated from high school and immediately began 
attending post-secondary schooling at University of Illinois at Champaign-Urbana, an accredited 
university, in 2016. PX11. K. graduated in Spring 2016 at the age of twenty-one. PX11 T. also 
went to college immediately after obtaining his high school diploma, attending Illinois State 
University, an accredited institution, beginning in Fall 2016 and graduating in Spring 2020 at the 
age of twenty-two. PX10; PX12 Neither K. nor T. pursued additional post-secondary education 
beyond obtaining their 4-year bachelor’s degrees. Their daughter, J., attended community college 
after graduating from high school for one year, at Joliet Community College, an accredited 
institution. PX13 J. then transferred to University of Iowa, also an accredited institution, in Fall 
2022 and her transcript records show attendance through Spring 2024. Id. According to Coda, J. 
has been in school continuously since high school and is currently preparing to enter her senior 
year at the age of twenty-one this Fall. Per Coda, J. is considering pursuing a graduate-level degree 
after graduating from University of Iowa. 
Coda was aware that an Estate had been opened for her husband in Will County, which 
was subsequently closed, but she does not recall who handled it. Coda herself filed a petition in 
the Court of Claims under the Line of Duty Compensation Act after her husband’s passing, 
wherein she represented herself for that separate cause of action. PX4; PX6; RX3. 
LODCA Hearing Testimony and Decision  
Coda brought a cause of action related to her husband’s passing under the Line of Duty 
Compensation Act (“LODCA”) before the Court of Claims, which proceeded to hearing October 
9, 2007, prior to and separate from proceeding to trial on the Workers’ Compensation matters 
herein. PX4; PX6; RX3

Consolidated Case: Robert Stephen Coda (deceased) by Widow Victoria L. Coda

Therein, Coda testified that her husband’s heart attack occurred while he was driving, but 
that the vehicle he was operating did not crash. PX6 at 39. Coda testified that her husband had 
been dealing with issues regarding revocations at work and that he was hitting “roadblocks” when 
trying to get the credit he was due for revenue obtained on those assignments. PX6 at 40-42. She 
also indicated that her husband would be exposed to “any range of stress” on a given day due to 
the type of work he performed. Id. at 39.  
Decedent’s former supervisor, Jeffrey Gaida, testified at the Court of Claims hearing. PX6 
at 23. Gaida had been Decedent’s acting supervisor at the time of his passing and knew Decedent 
since 1994. Id. at 13-14. Decedent worked typically 8:30am to 4:30pm and weekends when 
needed, and that Decedent worked on revocations two to three times a week, which could be 
interpreted as more stressful assignments because they were confrontational. Id. at 24-25, 27. 
Typically an agent would call Gaida in the morning and tell him where they were working that 
day. Id. at 27-28. Gaida testified that he did not see Decedent on the date of accident and did not 
know what assignment he was on. Id. at 17. He heard from another agent that Decedent had been 
at the Des Plaines office that morning and then left to do field work. Id. at 17. He had last seen 
Decedent on the prior Wednesday or Thursday of the previous week and did not notice anything 
remarkable about Decedent’s demeanor at that time. Id. at 20. Gaida did not recall any specifically 
egregious or stressful cases Decedent had been working on nor had Decedent ever complained to 
Gaida about any issues with his job. Id. at 19. 
Judge J. Sprague oversaw the LODCA hearing in the Court of Claims and found that Coda 
and Gaida did not testify that Decedent had looked stressed or was suffering from health problems 
due to job related stress. RX3 at 2. Judge Sprague opined that Decedent did not appear to be more 
stressed than usual in the months prior to his death according to testimony, and Gaida specifically 
did not recall Decedent complaining to him about any job-related stress. Id. No records were 
submitted into evidence regarding Decedent’s pre-2006 stent procedure or related follow-up 
cardiac care at the hearing and only partial ER records from January 23, 2006, and February 1, 
2006, were presented. RX3 at 3-4. Judge Sprague noted that there was a reference in the limited 
ER records to a stent ten years prior and a reference to Decedent taking Lipitor, a medication for 
high cholesterol, but the records did not clarify whether the stenting was specifically cardiac-
related. Judge Sprague further noted that it “would have greatly assisted” the court if expert

evidence had been provided to address whether Decedent’s heart attack was caused by job related 
stress, as well as providing expert insight as to the extent pre-existing medical conditions may 
have been relevant. Id. at 3. Citing these deficiencies in the record and being unable to speculate 
as to a pre-existing condition and how that might impact Decedent’s situation, Judge Sprague 
rendered a decision on the LODCA matter in Coda’s favor in the amount of $283,129.89. Id. at 
3-4, 6. 
Medical  
Prior to January 23, 2006, Decedent suffered an acute myocardial incident in 1996, which 
was treated with thrombolysis and two stents to the left anterior descending coronary artery. RX2 
at 1; PX14 at 179; 196-199. At that time, Decedent was noted to have a past history of high 
cholesterol and hypertension, and a family history of heart issues, including his father, brother, 
and possibly a grandparent having heart attacks. Id.; PX14 at 181. In December 2003, Decedent 
had a normal nuclear stress test, with no further cardiac symptoms or limitations. PX14 at 182, 
184; RX2 at 1; RX4 at 9-10. He was recommended for a routine stress test on February 17, 2004, 
and February 25, 2004, by Dr. Bliley, his provider at Heart Care Centers of Illinois, however those 
may not have been performed as there is no record of them in evidence. RX4 at 34-35. On July 
20, 2005, Dr. Bliley wrote a letter indicating that Decedent was due for a repeat stress test in 
December 2005 and that he would benefit from a 6-month cholesterol profile. Id. at 30. He was 
given Lipitor, Lisinopril, aspirin, and Toprol Xl. Id.  
On January 17, 2006, Petitioner was noted by Heart Care Centers of Illinois to be having 
trouble getting his stress test scheduled due to insurance approval issues and he was given an 
order from his provider to allow him to schedule his stress test at any hospital in the area. RX4 at 
9. He did not have his January 2006 stress test by the time of his January 23, 2006, incident, 
according to records in evidence. RX4 at 27; PX14 at 182. 
On January 23, 2006, Decedent was found unresponsive in his vehicle around 1:25 p.m. 
PX5. The records note that the car had slowed and gone off the road. Id. He was taken to Palos 
Community Hospital and found to have suffered a heart attack, an inferior non-ST-segment 
elevation myocardial infarction, resulting ultimately in severe anoxic brain injury. RX2 at 1-2;

RX4 at 27-28; PX14 at 217. Life support was eventually withdrawn and Decedent died on 
February 1, 2006. PX14 at 229; RX4 at 26.  
 
Evidence Deposition of Dr. Jeffrey Soble 
 
Dr. Jeffrey Soble testified at an evidence deposition on January 24, 2017, on behalf of 
Respondent. RX1. Dr. Soble is board certified in cardiovascular disease, echocardiography, and 
nuclear cardiology. Id. at 5-6. Dr. Soble authored a report on August 8, 2016, in which he had 
provided independent medical opinions related to Decedent’s 2006 heart attack. RX2. Dr. Soble 
opined in his report and maintained at his deposition that Decedent’s 2003 negative stress test 
would only have relevance to the year in which it was obtained and would not have much 
relevance to his 2006 heart attack. RX1 at 11-12; RX2. Dr. Soble opined that, in his medical 
experience, it is not uncommon to see someone with a normal stress test one year who presents 
with a heart attack several years later. RX1 at 12; RX2.  
Dr. Soble noted that there are well known and powerful risk factors for a myocardial 
infarction and Decedent had several of them. RX1 at 23, 27-28. These risk factors put Decedent 
at risk for a heart attack at any time and included a strong family history, a bad lipid profile even 
while taking Lipitor, hypertension, and a personal history of coronary artery disease. Id. He noted 
that there are no large-scale, randomized, controlled trials to assess that impact of job stress on 
coronary events. Id at 19. He opined that it is difficult to study scientifically compared to 
traditional risk factors. Id. at 19. Dr. Soble did not opine within a reasonable degree of medical 
and surgical certainty that stress was a cause of Decedent’s myocardial infarction on January 23, 
2006, but indicated that stress, including marital or work-related stress, could contribute to a heart 
attack in the same way that anything else in the universe could contribute to one. Id. at 29-30, 
RX2. Dr. Soble felt it was impossible to draw a connection between Decedent’s emotional state 
or any potential stress the Decedent may have felt and a myocardial infarction or to gage the 
impact stress may have had on a particular cardiac event because it would almost always be based 
on speculation. RX1 at 23-24; 26; 28-29. 
Evidence Deposition of Dr. Jason Robin 
Dr. Jason Robin testified at his evidence deposition on July 27, 2016, on behalf of 
Petitioner. PX7 Dr. Robin was board certified in cardiovascular disease, nuclear cardiology,

echocardiography, and vascular imaging. Id. at 5-6. Dr. Robin authored a Section 12 report on 
April 16, 2016. Id. at 8-9, 119. Dr. Robin opined that Decedent’s high cholesterol and genetic 
factors likely led to his premature coronary artery disease in 1996 when he was 39. Id. at 13-14. 
Dr. Robin also opined that Decedent’s work for IDOR contributed to the onset of his myocardial 
infarction on January 23, 2006. Id. at 13-14. Dr. Robin acknowledged that Decedent had an 
increased risk of dying from cardiac issues generally due to his pre-existing cardiovascular 
disease. Id. at 29-30. However, Dr. Robin still felt that stress was a factor in why this particular 
cardiac event occurred on January 23, 2006. Id. at 33.  
Dr. Robin based this conclusion on the facts that Decedent was driving a state-issued 
vehicle and working when the heart attack happened. Id. At 33. Dr. Robin opined that the stress 
of working, with the “police-like” duties his role required, would be a contributing factor to the 
plaque rupture which occurred in Decedent’s heart, triggering the January 2006 heart attack. Id. 
At 9-10, 35-36.  
Dr. Robin further opined that emotions are well known causes of acute cardiac disease. 
PX7 at 13-14; 16-18. Dr. Robin noted that he was relying particularly on his personal experience 
but also referencing specific medical literature that discussed acute emotional distress or anger 
episodes and their impact on myocardial infarctions. Id. At 13-14; 16-18.  
Dr. Robin did not assert that Decedent had sustained an acute work-related stress incident 
in this matter. PX7 at 35-26. Dr. Robin instead focused on the general stress caused by day-to-
day activities in the field, likening them to the general stress of being a lawyer, physician, or in 
any security and enforcement roles like a police officer. Id. At 35-36. Based on his impression 
that Decedent’s job was generally stressful in nature, Dr. Robin found the work stress to be a 
cause of the heart attack Decedent sustained January 23, 2006. Id. At 14-15, 121. Dr. Robin was 
asked whether he would still consider this heart attack to be work-related if Decedent had 
sustained his heart attack at home instead of while working, and he indicated that it would depend 
on what he had been doing at home when it occurred. Id. At 32.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
 
The Arbitrator adopts the above Findings of Fact in support of the Conclusions of Law set 
forth below.  
 
Issue C, whether the accident arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by 
Respondent, the Arbitrator finds as follows: 
 
The phrase "in the course of employment" refers to the time, place, and circumstances of 
the injury. McAllister v. Illinois Workers' Compensation Comm'n, 2020 IL 124848, ¶ 34. A 
compensable injury occurs 'in the course of' employment when it is sustained while he performs 
reasonable activities in conjunction with his employment. Id.  
"The 'arising out of' component is primarily concerned with causal connection. To satisfy 
this requirement it must be shown that the injury had its origin in some risk connected with, or 
incidental to, the employment so as to create a causal connection between the employment and the 
accidental injury." Id. at ¶ 36. To determine whether a claimant's injury arose out of his 
employment, the risks to which the claimant was exposed must be categorized. Id. The three 
categories of risks are "(1) risks distinctly associated with the employment; (2) risks personal to 
the employee; and (3) neutral risks which have no particular employment or personal 
characteristics." Id. at ¶ 38. “A risk is distinctly associated with an employee's employment if, at 
the time of the occurrence, the employee was performing (1) acts he or she was instructed to 
perform by the employer, (2) acts that he or she had a common-law or statutory duty to perform, 
or (3) acts that the employee might reasonably be expected to perform incident to his or her 
assigned duties.” Id. at ¶ 46.  
Pryor v. Illinois Workers' Compensation Comm'n, 2015 IL App (2d) 130874WC, ¶ 1, 27 
N.E.3d 678. The general rule is that an injury incurred by an employee in going to or returning 
from the place of employment does not arise out of or in the course of the employment and, hence, 
is not compensable. The rationale for this rule is that the employee's trip to and from work is the 
product of his own decision as to where he wants to live, a matter in which his employer ordinarily 
has no interest. An exception applies, however, when the employee is a "traveling employee." A 
"traveling employee" is one whose work duties require him to travel away from his employer's 
premises. Courts generally regard traveling employees differently from other employees when 
26IWCC0131

 
Consolidated Case: Robert Stephen Coda (deceased) by Widow Victoria L. Coda 
 
 
 
Case # 08 WC55917 
 
10 
 
considering whether an injury arose out of and in the course of employment. A traveling employee 
is deemed to be in the course of his employment from the time that he leaves home until he returns. 
An injury sustained by a traveling employee arises out of his employment if he was injured while 
engaging in conduct that was reasonable and foreseeable, i.e., conduct that might normally be 
anticipated or foreseen by the employer.  
Decedent was operating a State-owned vehicle and his duties required for him to travel 
away from his employer’s premises to the respective field locations to conduct investigations, 
revocations, and other assigned duties. 
Jeffrey Gaida, testified at the Court of Claims hearing that Decedent worked typically 8:30 
to 4:30pm and weekends when needed, and that Decedent worked on revocations two to three 
times a week. 
Gaida’s testimony was that he typically has his agents call in to report where they were 
going on any given day, but he did not have personal knowledge of where the Decedent was going 
or what assignment he was working on when he had his heart attack on the afternoon of January 
23, 2006.  
Coda testified at the Court of Claims hearing that her husband’s heart attack occurred while 
he was driving, but that the vehicle he was operating did not crash. Coda testified that her husband 
had been dealing with issues regarding revocations at work. 
Suoranta recalled that Decedent left the office on January 23, 2006, and she assumed he 
went out on assignment, but admitted that she did not know what assignment he may have been 
given that date, whether it involved a revocation or where he was going.  
On January 23, 2006, Decedent was found unresponsive in his vehicle around 1:25 p.m. 
The records note that the car had slowed and gone off the road. He was taken to Palos Community 
Hospital and found to have suffered a heart attack, an inferior non-ST-segment elevation 
myocardial infarction, resulting ultimately in severe anoxic brain injury. 
Although none of the aforementioned testimony definitively showed what Decedent was 
doing or where he was travelling to at the time on the afternoon of January 23, 2006, it can be 
reasonably and foreseeably anticipated that because his duties required him to drive to the field 
locations to perform investigations and that it happened during his typical work hours, his conduct 
falls within the traveling employee exception in “Pryor”.

Issue F, whether Petitioner’s current condition of ill-being is causally related to the injury, the 
Arbitrator finds as follows:  
 
To obtain compensation under the Act, a claimant must prove that some act or phase of his 
employment was a causative factor in his ensuing injuries. A work-related injury need not be the 
sole or principal causative factor, as long as it was a causative factor in the resulting condition of 
ill-being. Even if the claimant had a preexisting degenerative condition which made him more 
vulnerable to injury, recovery for an accidental injury will not be denied as long as he can show 
that his employment was also a causative factor. Thus, a claimant may establish a causal 
connection in such cases if he can show that a work-related injury played a role in aggravating his 
preexisting condition. Sisbro, Inc. v. Industrial Comm'n, 207 Ill. 2d 193, 205, 797 N.E.2d 665, 
278 Ill. Dec. 70 (2003).  
The courts have awarded compensability in matters where continuing mental stress was 
found to have resulted in a physical injury, not unlike repetitive physical injuries. Baggett v. Indus. 
Comm'n (marion Cmty. Sch. Dist. No. 2), 201 Ill. 2d 187, 775 N.E.2d 908, 2002 Ill. LEXIS 291, 
266 Ill. Dec. 836, 13 A.L.R.6th 787.  
In this case, the evidence shows that Decedent performed work which could be considered 
generally stressful. Jeffrey Gaida, testified at the Court of Claims hearing that Decedent worked 
on revocations two to three times a week, which could be interpreted as more stressful 
assignments because they were confrontational. 
Although Coda had no first-hand knowledge of Decedent’s responsibilities at IDOR, she 
testified that Decedent’s job seemed to become more demanding between 2005 to 2006, as she 
recalled that he was spending more time after normal work hours logging his assignment notes and 
was working later, causing them to hold dinner for him frequently.  Moreover, Coda testified that 
her husband had been dealing with issues regarding revocations at work and that he was hitting 
“roadblocks” when trying to get the credit he was due for revenue obtained on those assignments. 
PX6 at 40-42. She also indicated that her husband would be exposed to “any range of stress” on a 
given day due to the type of work he performed. Id. at 39.

Suoranta testified that, at times, revocations could be more stressful assignments because 
of the reactions of business owners to the revocation process. Suoranta never performed 
“revocations” during her tenure with IDOR. She testified that Decedent had worked on 
revocations but that she did not know the volume of revocation assignments he worked. She saw 
Decedent in the office that morning and he “seemed fine,” with “nothing unusual to note.” 
In the Court of Claims’ case, Judge Sprague opined that Decedent did not appear to be 
more stressed than usual in the months prior to his death according to testimony, and Gaida 
specifically did not recall Decedent complaining to him about any job-related stress. 
Dr. Robin opined that Decedent’s high cholesterol and genetic factors likely led to his 
premature coronary artery disease in 1996 when he was 39. Id. at 13-14. Dr. Robin also opined 
that Decedent’s work for IDOR contributed to the onset of his myocardial infarction on January 
23, 2006. Id. at 13-14. Dr. Robin acknowledged that Decedent had an increased risk of dying 
from cardiac issues generally due to his pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Id. at 29-30. 
However, Dr. Robin still felt that stress was a factor in why this particular cardiac event occurred 
on January 23, 2006. Id. at 33. Dr. Robin based this conclusion on the facts that Decedent was 
driving a state-issued vehicle and working when the heart attack happened. Id. at 33. Dr. Robin 
opined that the stress of working, with the “police-like” duties his role required, would be a 
contributing factor to the plaque rupture which occurred in Decedent’s heart, triggering the 
January 2006 heart attack. Id. at 9-10, 35-36.  
Dr. Robin further opined that emotions are well known causes of acute cardiac disease. 
PX7 at 13-14; 16-18. Dr. Robin noted that he was relying particularly on his personal experience 
but also referencing specific medical literature that discussed acute emotional distress or anger 
episodes and their impact on myocardial infarctions. Id. at 13-14; 16-18.  
Dr. Robin did not assert that Decedent had sustained an acute work-related stress incident 
in this matter. PX7 at 35-26. Dr. Robin instead focused on the general stress caused by day-to-day 
activities in the field, likening them to the general stress of being a lawyer, physician, or in any 
security and enforcement roles like a police officer. Id. at 35-36. Based on his impression that 
Decedent’s job was generally stressful in nature, Dr. Robin found the work stress to be a cause of 
the heart attack Decedent sustained January 23, 2006. Id. at 14-15, 121. Dr. Robin was asked 
whether he would still consider this heart attack to be work-related if Decedent had sustained his

heart attack at home instead of while working, and he indicated that it would depend on what he 
had been doing at home when it occurred. Id. at 32. The Arbitrator notes that Dr. Robin’s opinion 
hinges on Decedent’s work stress but Dr. Robin refers only to his “impression” that Decedent 
worked a stressful job based on the nature of his position. 
In contrast, Dr. Soble indicated that stress, including marital or work-related stress, could 
contribute to a heart attack in the same way that anything else in the universe could contribute to 
one. Dr. Soble felt it was impossible to draw a connection between Decedent’s emotional state or 
any potential stress the Decedent may have felt and a myocardial infarction or to gage the impact 
stress may have had on a particular cardiac event because it would almost always be based on 
speculation. 
Based on the record as a whole, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner’s death on February 1, 
2006, is causally related to the Petitioner’s myocardial infarction sustained on January 23, 2006. 
In support of the Arbitrator’s finding, the Arbitrator weighed the testimony of Gaida, Coda, 
Suoranta and Dr. Robin against the opinions and findings of Dr. Soble and Judge Sprague (Court 
of Claims).  
Thus, the Arbitrator finds the testimony of Gaida, Coda, Suoranta coupled with Dr. Robin’s 
opinions and findings, to be more persuasive than those of Dr. Soble and Judge Sprague. Although 
Dr. Soble opined that it is “impossible” to gage the impact stress had on Petitioner’s cardiac event, 
because doing so would be based on speculation, he conceded that work-related stress could 
contribute to a heart attack. Overall, the Arbitrator can reasonably infer that Petitioner was under 
work-related stress and that stress was a contributing cause that led to Petitioner’s death on 
February 1, 2006.
